stated: Reform UK will cut residential stamp duty to 0% below £750,000, 2% from £750,000-£1.5 million, and 4% over £1.5 million, aiming to boost economic activity and housebuilding.

source.quote: Cut Residential Stamp Duty Substantially boost economic activity and housebuilding by cutting Stamp Duty to 0% below £750k. Cut it to 2% from £750k - £1.5m and cut it to 4% over £1.5m.

bearing_set.reason: Stamp duty cuts directly affect the cost of home purchase and market mobility; the key contested question is whether the saving is capitalised into higher house prices (worsening affordability) or genuinely helps buyers and spurs supply — a non-negligible verdict on the affordable-housing fundamental.
A direct reduction in stamp duty lowers the tax burden on homebuyers at point of transaction, improving take-home value of the purchase for those who buy.
SDLT raises ~£15bn/yr; substantially cutting rates without a stated offsetting revenue source materially widens the funding gap and worsens debt-path sustainability.
Lower transaction costs reduce the 'lock-in' effect of stamp duty, potentially improving labour mobility and housing market dynamism — a genuine prosperity mechanism cited by IFS/OBR analysis.

Buyers below the current 0% threshold (~£250k) gain nothing; gains accrue to mid-to-high value purchasers, and renters are excluded entirely — the distributional incidence skews toward wealthier households, widening the wealth gap.

membership_note: Five fundamentals clear the non-negligible bar: O1 (price-capitalisation risk), O11 (direct tax reduction), O12 (revenue loss), O13 (mobility/dynamism), and O14 (regressive distributional incidence). The stated housebuilding aim is speculative and does not offset the demand-side housing-affordability concern on O1.
